## Root Cause Analysis

I hit the same issue with GitHub shorthand plugins (`Edison-A-N/opencode-preview`). Traced it to commit `c9326fc19` (PR #18308 — "refactor: replace BunProc with Npm module using @npmcli/arborist").

### The bug

In `Npm.add()` → `resolveEntryPoint()`, after arborist installs a dependency, `loadVirtual()` is called and `first.path` returns the **wrapper directory** (e.g. `~/.cache/opencode/packages/Edison-A-N/opencode-preview/`) instead of the actual package directory (`~/.cache/opencode/packages/Edison-A-N/opencode-preview/node_modules/opencode-preview/`).

This means `readPluginPackage(target)` reads the wrapper `package.json`:
```json
{"dependencies":{"opencode-preview":"github:Edison-A-N/opencode-preview"}}
```
...which has no exports, no main — so plugin resolution fails.

For GitHub shorthand specs, there's a second issue: `npa("Edison-A-N/opencode-preview")` parses as a GitHub type where `hit.name` is `null`. The fallback in `resolvePluginTarget` uses the raw spec string as the package name, producing an impossible path like `node_modules/Edison-A-N/package.json`.

### Log

```
ERROR service=plugin path=Edison-A-N/opencode-preview error=ENOENT: no such file or directory, open '/home/user/.cache/opencode/packages/Edison-A-N/opencode-preview/node_modules/Edison-A-N/package.json' failed to resolve plugin server entry
```

### Reproduction

1. Add `"Edison-A-N/opencode-preview"` (or any GitHub shorthand) to `opencode.json` plugins
2. Start opencode — plugin fails to load

### Environment

Thanks bot — cross-checked all three and I think the likely shared root cause sits in how the frontend tracks per-agent selected model state, and specifically how it decides whether to send `input.model` on each submission.

All four issues (this one plus #21351, #6636, #23369) are different triggers of the same underlying asymmetry around `packages/opencode/src/session/prompt.ts:932`:

```ts
const model = input.model ?? ag.model ?? (yield* lastModel(input.sessionID))
```

The backend fallback order is fine in isolation. What varies across these issues is whether the frontend correctly sends `input.model` on a given submission:

- **#23666 (this issue)**: UI drops `input.model` on message 2 of a new session, exactly once
- **#21351**: UI drops `input.model` on Tab-switch between Plan/Build, so each mode re-resolves to the new agent's `ag.model`
- **#23369**: Session resume only restores one agent's selected model; other agents re-resolve to `ag.model` on switch
- **#6636** goes in the opposite direction (subagent's model bleeding into main agent). Without reading that code path I can't say if it's the same state map, but it's clearly in the same "per-agent selected model state" problem area — possibly the same map written with the wrong agent key

Net: these look like four symptoms of one missing invariant — **"each agent in a session has its own persistent `selectedModel` state, independent of `ag.model`, surviving first-message completion, mode switches, subagent dispatch, and session resume"**. Fixing that one invariant should close this whole cluster.

Happy to keep these linked; feel free to triage this as a cluster under a single model-selection-persistence umbrella if that fits the roadmap better.

A related UX reference from Codex: it has a `/side` command that opens a temporary side conversation instead of immediately pushing the current selection/problem into the main thread.

I think the same design principle applies here:
- keep normal text selection/copy as the default
- make `Add to chat` / `Quick edit` explicit actions
- and optionally let those actions target a temporary side session instead of the main chat

That would preserve standard selection behavior while still supporting fast contextual actions. In many cases, “ask about this selection in a side thread” feels safer and less disruptive than immediately injecting it into the primary conversation.

A concrete reference point here: Codex has a `/side` command for this exact class of workflow.

`/side` starts a temporary side conversation from the current thread, with inherited history available as reference, while keeping the main thread focused. In practice it is useful for things like:
- commit / staging / publish prep
- quick investigation or codebase exploration
- follow-up questions that are useful but not part of the main problem-solving thread

What I like about that model is that it is not just “fork for alternative ideas”. It is specifically a lightweight child thread for context-heavy side work, so the primary thread does not get polluted.

If OpenCode already has parent/child session infrastructure and subagent session navigation, a first-class UX around this kind of temporary side session could be very valuable.
